subject: Astronomy
title: Phases of the Moon
intro: The Moon does not make its own light; it shines because it reflects sunlight toward Earth.

facts.text: The Moon orbits Earth, and half of it is always lit by the Sun, but the part of that lit half we can see changes as it moves.
facts.ev: The Moon orbits Earth, and the part of its lit half that we can see changes as it moves.

facts.text: A full cycle of phases, from one new moon to the next, takes about 29 days.
facts.ev: A full cycle of phases, from one new moon to the next, takes about 29 days.

facts.text: During a new moon, the lit side faces away from Earth, so the Moon is nearly invisible in the night sky.
facts.ev: During a new moon, the lit side faces away from Earth, so the Moon is nearly invisible in the night sky.

facts.text: At full moon, we see the whole lit side of the Moon, and it appears as a bright circle.
facts.ev: At full moon, we see the whole lit side of the Moon as a bright circle.

facts.text: The Moon's surface is covered in craters formed by rocks that crashed into it long ago.
facts.ev: The Moon's surface is covered in craters formed by rocks that crashed into it long ago.

facts.text: Gravity on the Moon is about one sixth as strong as gravity on Earth.
facts.ev: Gravity on the Moon is about one sixth as strong as gravity on Earth.

facts.text: Ocean tides rise and fall mainly because of the pull of the Moon's gravity on Earth's water.
facts.ev: Ocean tides rise and fall mainly because of the pull of the Moon's gravity on Earth's water.

facts.text: People have used the repeating phases of the Moon to build calendars for thousands of years.
facts.ev: The source mentions that people have used the repeating phases of the Moon to build calendars for thousands of years.

models.q: Why does the Moon look different from night to night?
models.restate: The Moon's appearance changes from one night to the next.
models.answer: The Moon looks different because we see a different amount of its sunlit side as it travels around Earth.
exp: Since the Moon keeps moving along its path, the angle from which we view its bright half is always changing.
When the bright half points away from us, almost nothing of the Moon can be seen, which is the darkest point of its cycle.
rep: The Moon orbits Earth, and the visible part of its lit half changes as it moves.
A new moon happens when the lit side faces away from Earth, so the Moon is almost invisible.
models.sum: The Moon's changing look comes from how much of its lit half faces Earth as it orbits.
models.sumNew: The Moon's changing look comes from how much of its lit half faces Earth, and its surface is covered with craters formed long ago.
models.bad: The Moon looks different because Earth's shadow slowly covers a little more of it each night.
models.badRestate: The Moon's surface looks different up close because of its many craters.
models.offExp: The marks left by past collisions explain why the Moon's surface looks rough up close.

models.q: How can the repeating pattern of the Moon's phases be useful to people?
models.restate: The repeating pattern of the Moon's phases can serve people in practical ways.
models.answer: The regular pattern of phases is useful because it lets people predict the Moon's appearance and keep track of time.
exp: Because each cycle lasts about the same length, anyone who counts nights can estimate when the next new moon will arrive.
Since the same cycle returns again and again, people could count on it as a dependable way to organize their months.
rep: One cycle from a new moon to the next lasts about 29 days.
Calendars have been based on the Moon's repeating phases for thousands of years.
models.sum: Overall, the Moon's predictable cycle gives people a natural way to anticipate its appearance and measure the passing of time.
models.sumNew: Overall, the Moon's predictable cycle helps people measure time, and the Moon's gravity is about one sixth as strong as Earth's.
models.bad: The Moon's phases are useful because they control when each season begins on Earth.
models.badRestate: The Moon's gravity is much weaker than Earth's, which affects how objects behave there.
models.offExp: Because the Moon's gravity is weaker, an object there would weigh less than it does on Earth.

subject: Plants and animals
title: Desert cacti
intro: Cacti are plants that grow in deserts, where rain is rare and the sun is strong.

facts.text: A cactus stem is thick and spongy, and it stores large amounts of water after a rainfall.
facts.ev: The thick, spongy stem of a cactus stores large amounts of water after a rainfall.

facts.text: Instead of broad leaves, a cactus has narrow spines, which lose much less water to the dry air.
facts.ev: A cactus has narrow spines instead of broad leaves, so it loses much less water to the dry air.

facts.text: Many cacti have shallow roots that spread wide near the surface and quickly soak up rain before it dries up.
facts.ev: Many cacti have shallow roots that spread wide near the surface and quickly soak up rain.

facts.text: Spines also provide a little shade and keep some animals from eating the plant.
facts.ev: Spines also provide a little shade and keep some animals from eating the plant.

facts.text: Some cacti can survive for a year or more without any rain.
facts.ev: Some cacti can survive for a year or more without any rain.

facts.text: The tallest cactus, the saguaro, can grow taller than a house with two stories.
facts.ev: The saguaro, the tallest cactus, can grow taller than a house with two stories.

facts.text: Cactus flowers often open at night and are pollinated by bats and moths.
facts.ev: Cactus flowers often open at night and are pollinated by bats and moths.

facts.text: People grow cacti in pots because they need very little watering.
facts.ev: People grow cacti in pots because they need very little watering.

models.q: How is a cactus able to survive in a desert?
models.restate: A cactus is able to live in a place that gets very little rain.
models.answer: A cactus survives in the desert because its body is built to store water and to lose very little of it.
exp: Having a reserve of stored water allows the plant to keep living through the long periods between rainstorms.
With less water escaping through spines than broad leaves would allow, the plant keeps more of what it has stored.
rep: After a rainfall, the thick, spongy stem of a cactus holds a large amount of water.
A cactus has narrow spines instead of broad leaves, so it loses less water to dry air.
models.sum: A cactus survives desert conditions because it keeps a supply of water and wastes very little.
models.sumNew: A cactus survives desert conditions by keeping water, and its flowers often open at night for bats and moths.
models.bad: A cactus survives in the desert because its roots reach water hundreds of feet underground.
models.badRestate: Cactus flowers often open at night, which helps the plant get pollinated.
models.offExp: Flowers that open at night can attract nighttime visitors such as bats and moths.

models.q: Why can a cactus make good use of a brief rainstorm?
models.restate: A cactus is able to benefit from rain that lasts only a short time.
models.answer: A cactus uses a brief storm well because it absorbs water quickly and holds on to what it takes in.
exp: Roots that stay near the surface and spread wide catch the water as soon as it soaks into the soil, before the sun dries it out.
Because the stem keeps the absorbed water inside, the plant can use it slowly after the storm is over.
rep: Shallow roots spread wide near the surface and soak up rain for many cacti.
A cactus stem is thick and spongy and stores large amounts of water after rainfall.
models.sum: A cactus makes the most of short storms by soaking up water fast and storing it for later.
models.sumNew: A cactus makes the most of short storms by soaking up water fast, and its spines also keep some animals from eating it.
models.bad: A cactus uses brief storms well because its spines can make rain fall on the plant.
models.badRestate: Spines help protect a cactus by keeping some animals from eating it.
models.offExp: Since spines cast a little shade, the plant's surface stays slightly cooler in the strong sun.

subject: Physics
title: Levers
intro: A lever is a simple machine made of a stiff bar that turns around a fixed point called a fulcrum.

facts.text: When the fulcrum is close to the load, a small push far from the fulcrum can lift a heavy object.
facts.ev: When the fulcrum is close to the load, a small push far from the fulcrum can lift a heavy object.

facts.text: A crowbar lets a person pry up a nail by pushing down on the long end of the bar.
facts.ev: A person can pry up a nail with a crowbar by pushing down on the long end of the bar.

facts.text: A seesaw is a lever with the fulcrum in the middle, so two children of equal weight can balance each other.
facts.ev: A seesaw is a lever with its fulcrum in the middle, so two children of equal weight can balance.

facts.text: The farther you push from the fulcrum, the less force you need, but you must move your hand through a longer distance.
facts.ev: The text states that pushing farther from the fulcrum takes less force, but the hand must move through a longer distance.

facts.text: Scissors are made of two levers joined at a shared fulcrum.
facts.ev: Scissors are made of two levers joined at a shared fulcrum.

facts.text: People have used levers for thousands of years to move heavy stones.
facts.ev: People have used levers for thousands of years to move heavy stones.

facts.text: A wheelbarrow is a lever with the fulcrum at the wheel, so the person lifting the handles carries only part of the load.
facts.ev: A wheelbarrow is a lever with the fulcrum at the wheel, so the person lifting the handles carries only part of the load.

facts.text: A lever does not create energy; it only changes how effort is applied.
facts.ev: A lever does not create energy; it only changes how effort is applied.

models.q: How does a lever make heavy objects easier to lift?
models.restate: A lever changes how much effort a person needs to lift a heavy object.
models.answer: A lever makes lifting easier by letting a small force applied far from the fulcrum move a heavy load.
exp: Placing the fulcrum near the load gives the person leverage, so a little effort becomes a large lifting force.
The nail resists being pulled out, yet the long end of the bar lets a modest push overcome that resistance.
rep: A small push far from a fulcrum that is close to the load can lift a heavy object.
A crowbar lets someone push down on its long end to pry up a nail.
models.sum: In short, a lever helps by turning a small push far from the fulcrum into enough force to move a heavy load.
models.sumNew: In short, a lever turns a small push into enough force to move a heavy load, and a seesaw is a lever with its fulcrum in the middle.
models.bad: A lever makes lifting easier by creating extra energy that the person did not supply.
models.badRestate: A seesaw balances two children by placing a fulcrum between them.
models.offExp: Because the fulcrum is in the middle, a seesaw balances when the weights on both sides match.

models.q: What does a person give up when a lever makes a task need less force?
models.restate: It is worth understanding what a person gives up when a lever lowers the force a task needs.
models.answer: A person gives up distance, because the easier the push becomes, the farther the hand must travel.
exp: Since the hand must travel through a longer distance, the smaller force is paid for with extra motion.
Because no energy is created, the lever cannot reduce the force a person needs without asking for something in return.
rep: Pushing farther from the fulcrum takes less force but a longer movement of the hand.
A lever only changes how effort is applied and does not create energy.
models.sum: A lever trades force for distance rather than producing any extra energy.
models.sumNew: A lever trades force for distance, and scissors use two levers that share a fulcrum.
models.bad: A person gives up strength, because using a lever always makes the user weaker over time.
models.badRestate: Scissors use two levers that share a fulcrum, which gives them cutting power.
models.offExp: Because the two blades pivot on one shared point, they cut by squeezing the material between them.

subject: Transportation
title: Bicycle gears
intro: Most bicycles have gears, which are wheels with teeth that connect the pedals to the back wheel by a chain.

facts.text: In a low gear, each turn of the pedals moves the bike only a short distance, which makes pedaling easier on a steep hill.
facts.ev: In a low gear, each turn of the pedals moves the bike only a short distance, which makes a steep hill easier to climb.

facts.text: In a high gear, each turn of the pedals moves the bike a long distance, so a rider can reach a high speed on flat ground.
facts.ev: In a high gear, each turn of the pedals moves the bike a long distance, so a rider can reach a high speed on flat ground.

facts.text: A rider changes gears by moving a lever that shifts the chain from one toothed wheel to another.
facts.ev: A rider changes gears by moving a lever that shifts the chain from one toothed wheel to another.

facts.text: Many bikes have between seven and twenty-one gear combinations.
facts.ev: Many bikes have between seven and twenty-one gear combinations.

facts.text: A good gear choice lets a rider keep pedaling at a steady, comfortable pace.
facts.ev: A good gear choice lets a rider keep pedaling at a steady, comfortable pace.

facts.text: Bicycle helmets are designed to absorb impact and protect the head.
facts.ev: Bicycle helmets are designed to absorb impact and protect the head.

facts.text: The first bicycles, built in the early 1800s, had no pedals at all and were pushed along by the rider's feet.
facts.ev: The first bicycles, built in the early 1800s, had no pedals and were pushed along by the rider's feet.

facts.text: Chains are usually oiled so they move smoothly across the teeth.
facts.ev: Chains are usually oiled so they move smoothly across the teeth.

models.q: Why do bicycles have more than one gear?
models.restate: Many bicycles come with several gears instead of just one.
models.answer: Bicycles have several gears so riders can adjust how hard they pedal for different kinds of ground.
exp: On a steep hill, an easier gear keeps the rider from having to push very hard just to keep climbing.
On level ground, a harder gear turns each pedal stroke into more distance, letting the rider build up speed.
rep: A low gear moves the bike a short distance with each turn of the pedals.
A high gear moves the bike a long distance with each turn of the pedals.
models.sum: In short, several gears let a rider match the effort of pedaling to hills and flat roads alike.
models.sumNew: In short, several gears let a rider match effort to the road, and the first bicycles from the early 1800s had no pedals.
models.bad: Bicycles have several gears because the chain would break if it only used one.
models.badRestate: The first bicycles looked very different from the ones people ride today.
models.offExp: Since early bicycles had no pedals, riders had to push themselves along with their feet.

models.q: How does choosing the right gear help a rider stay comfortable?
models.restate: The gear a rider chooses can affect how comfortable a ride feels.
models.answer: The right gear keeps the effort of pedaling steady, whatever the slope of the road.
exp: Pedaling at a steady pace avoids sudden bursts of effort that would tire a rider quickly.
Making each turn easier on a hill keeps the rider's pace from slowing to a struggle.
rep: A good gear lets a rider keep a steady, comfortable pedaling pace.
A low gear moves the bike a short distance per pedal turn on a steep hill.
models.sum: Choosing a gear to suit the slope lets a rider pedal at a steady and comfortable pace.
models.sumNew: Choosing a gear to suit the slope keeps pedaling comfortable, and chains are usually oiled to move smoothly.
models.bad: The right gear keeps a rider comfortable because it makes the bicycle weigh less on hills.
models.badRestate: Oiling a bicycle chain helps it move smoothly across the teeth.
models.offExp: Oil reduces friction, so the chain slides over the teeth with less resistance.

subject: Chemistry
title: Rust and iron
intro: Rust is the reddish-brown coating that can appear on objects made of iron or steel.

facts.text: Rust forms when iron reacts with oxygen in the presence of water.
facts.ev: Rust forms when iron reacts with oxygen in the presence of water.
facts.tag: iron reacting with oxygen and water

facts.text: Rust is weaker than iron, so a badly rusted object can crumble or break.
facts.ev: Rust is weaker than iron, so a badly rusted object can crumble or break.

facts.text: Painting a metal object keeps water and air away from the iron underneath.
facts.ev: Paint on a metal object keeps water and air away from the iron underneath.

facts.text: Rust forms faster in damp places, and salty seawater makes the process even quicker.
facts.ev: Rust forms faster in damp places, and salty seawater makes the process even quicker.

facts.text: Stainless steel contains chromium, which forms a thin protective layer on the surface.
facts.ev: Stainless steel contains chromium, which forms a thin protective layer on its surface.

facts.text: Steel is made mostly of iron, with small amounts of other materials added.
facts.ev: Steel is made mostly of iron, with small amounts of other materials added.

facts.text: Some metals, such as gold, do not rust at all.
facts.ev: Some metals, such as gold, do not rust at all.

facts.text: Gardeners often wipe their tools dry and coat them with oil after using them.
facts.ev: Gardeners often wipe their tools dry and coat them with oil after use.

models.q: What causes rust to form on an iron object?
models.restate: Rust forming on an iron object has a specific cause that can be identified.
models.answer: Rust forms when iron is exposed to both oxygen and water.
exp: Since iron, oxygen, and water must all meet, an iron object kept dry is much less likely to rust.
Damp air and salty water supply the moisture that speeds up the change, so objects near the sea rust quickly.
rep: Iron reacts with oxygen in the presence of water to form rust.
Rust forms faster in damp places, and salty seawater speeds it up even more.
models.sum: Rust develops when iron meets oxygen and water, and extra moisture makes it happen faster.
models.sumNew: Rust develops when iron meets oxygen and water, but gold avoids the problem because it does not rust.
models.bad: Rust forms when iron is heated until it glows red-hot in the open air.
models.badRestate: Some metals never rust, no matter how long they are left outside.
models.offExp: Because gold does not rust, it can keep its shine without any protection.

models.q: How can people protect iron objects from rust?
models.restate: People can take steps to keep iron objects from rusting.
models.answer: People protect iron by keeping water and oxygen from reaching its surface.
exp: Because rust needs both water and air, a coating that blocks them stops the change before it starts.
The thin layer formed by chromium acts like a built-in coating, so stainless steel protects itself.
rep: Painting a metal object keeps water and air away from the iron below.
Stainless steel contains chromium, which forms a thin layer on the surface.
models.sum: Blocking the contact between iron and the water and air it needs is how rust can be prevented.
models.sumNew: Blocking the contact between iron and the water and air it needs prevents rust, and rusted iron is weaker than ordinary iron.
models.bad: People protect iron by leaving it in damp, salty places so that rust cannot spread.
models.badRestate: Rust damages iron objects by making them weaker over time.
models.offExp: Since rust is weaker than iron, a badly rusted beam may no longer hold as much weight.
